findings.claim: Corporate culture as the medium of engagement. ... Engagement happens through culture even when individual interactions are absent. (Source: Ch 6.4)

findings.claim: Unions represent ~10.7% of US workers. Collective bargaining produces a labor agreement with terms governing wages, benefits, work conditions, grievance handling, and dispute resolution.
findings.failure_mode: 10.7% is union membership in 2017, not representation, and the year is dropped. The source's contract list is union security, management rights, wages, benefits and job security; grievance handling is a separate process (Ch 8.8), not listed as a contract term.
findings.evidence: Deep 363, 367. Source 21990-22003 ('typically covers such issues as union security, management rights, wages, benefits, and job security'), 22133.
findings.fix: correct: Union membership fell to 10.7% of workers (14.8 million) in 2017. Collective bargaining produces a labor agreement that typically covers union security, management rights, wages, benefits and job security; grievances follow a separate step-by-step procedure (Ch 8.8).

findings.claim: Pay/reward systems disconnected from engagement quality. Equity theory predicts disengagement when the link between effort, performance, and reward is unclear.
findings.failure_mode: Wrong theory for the mechanism: the effort-performance-reward links are expectancy theory. Equity theory is about outcome-to-input comparisons with a referent.
findings.evidence: Deep 391 (expectancy: effort-to-performance, performance-to-outcome, outcomes-to-needs), 392 (equity).
findings.fix: correct: Expectancy theory predicts weak motivation when the links from effort to performance to valued outcome are unclear; equity theory predicts reduced effort, raise requests, distorted perceptions or exit when employees see their outcome-to-input ratio as unfair (Ch 9.6).

notes: The distillation looks templated on the OpenStax Organizational Behavior stakeholder distillation. A cluster of OB/PoM concepts appears as if this source carried them: process vs relationship conflict, BATNA, distributive vs integrative negotiation, power-base outcomes (commitment/compliance), procedural justice, open systems, groupthink/devil's advocate, bounded rationality, time/goal orientations, coalitions, and the Mintzberg and French-and-Raven attributions. None are in the converted source (each grep = 0 hits); all are in the OB and/or PoM deep refs. The Carroll misattribution again runs through the file and a concept anchor (`carrolls-pyramid`). Structural defects, not graded as claims: (a) the Integration table names concepts, not corpus references, in 10 of 11 rows; (b) an orphan Integration row ('Annual report and financial transparency') sits at line 229 after the Evidence-marker section; (c) the scope is open, but the distillation carries no verbatim blockquotes, only inline [V] quotes, where the protocol asks for 2-5 blockquotes. All inline [V] quotations were checked word-for-word against the converted source: stakeholders (5548), CSR (5386-5387, both clauses), leadership (15860), power (15890-15891), culture (17321-17322), retention (29657), customer satisfaction (29607-29608), canned presentations (34483). All exact except the trimmed stakeholder list at line 14. The '16 [BT] markers' count at 228 is correct. The worked-example figures (45 employees, 3,000 weekly customers) are scenario-internal. Claim count is approximate (about 162 discrete claims); grouped findings list their repeated lines in the section field.
